idea.text: FieldNote: a phone app for owners of small landscaping crews (2 to 8 people) in Poland. The crew lead photographs the site before and after, taps start and stop per job, and the owner gets a ready invoice the same evening with photos attached. Today most owners write hours in a notebook or a WhatsApp group and invoice a week later, which means arguments about what was done and late payments. Price: 29 EUR per month per company, flat. I ran a crew like this for six years and still know about 40 owners in my region. First channel: I will call them, then the regional trade group on Facebook. Stage: idea and a clickable prototype, evenings only, no outside money.

answers.today: Notebook, WhatsApp photos, invoice in a spreadsheet template a week later.
answers.stage: Clickable prototype, about 8 hours a week, can go a year without revenue.

evidence: invoice a week later, which means arguments about what was done and late payments
write hours in a notebook or a WhatsApp group
assumptions: Assuming a late invoice delays payment by one to three weeks for a crew that bills a few thousand EUR a month.
rubrics.reasoning: The text names a recurring cost: disputes over work done and late payments, both tied to invoicing a week after the job. That is weekly pain with a cash-flow cost, which matches the 4 anchor. It is not a 5 because the cost is described, not quantified; nothing says how often disputes happen or how much cash sits unpaid.
questions: How many invoices a month end in an argument about scope?
How many days late do customers pay on average?
improve: Lead with the cash-flow number: days from job to money, before and after.

evidence: owners of small landscaping crews (2 to 8 people) in Poland
I ran a crew like this for six years and still know about 40 owners in my region
assumptions: Assuming the owner both decides and pays, which is normal at this size.
rubrics.reasoning: A narrow segment, a named buyer who is also the user, and a concrete way to reach the first forty of them. Owners at this size already pay for phones, fuel and some software, so a monthly fee is within their budgeting. This matches the 5 anchor. The only open point is whether the forty owners are representative of the country.
questions: Of the 40 owners you know, how many still run crews of 2 to 8?

evidence: small landscaping crews (2 to 8 people) in Poland
assumptions: Assuming 15 000 to 30 000 landscaping businesses in Poland with 2 to 8 people; the text gives no count.
Assuming 5 percent of them would adopt any app in two years.
rubrics.reasoning: Bottom-up: assuming 20 000 crews of this size times 29 EUR times 12 months gives a ceiling near 7 million EUR a year, and a reachable 5 percent is about 350 000 EUR a year. That supports a small company, not a venture outcome. Why now is not stated; smartphones on site have been normal for years. The category is stable rather than growing. Score 3: real but not sized by the text.
questions: How many landscaping companies of this size exist in Poland (GUS data by employment band)?
What changed recently that makes owners want this now?
improve: State the target: a lifestyle business at 300 crews, or a path to adjacent trades (cleaning, roofing) that lifts the ceiling.

evidence: write hours in a notebook or a WhatsApp group and invoice a week later
Notebook, WhatsApp photos, invoice in a spreadsheet template a week later.
assumptions: From general knowledge: field-service tools (Jobber, Workiz) and Polish invoicing apps exist, but target larger teams or only the invoice step.
rubrics.reasoning: The status quo is named precisely, and the switching reason is concrete: the invoice goes out the same evening with photos instead of a week later. Switching cost is low because the crew already takes photos on phones. The text does not name any competing app, which keeps this from a 5; the founder should check what the owners who already use software use.
questions: Which three apps have the owners you know tried and dropped, and why?
improve: Position against the notebook, not against software: same-evening invoice with proof.

evidence: 29 EUR per month per company, flat
assumptions: Assuming a crew bills 5 000 to 15 000 EUR a month, so 29 EUR is under 1 percent of revenue.
Assuming cost to serve is under 2 EUR a month per company (storage for photos, no model calls).
rubrics.reasoning: Flat per-company pricing fits how a small owner budgets and avoids per-seat friction for a crew that changes size by season. Against the pain (late payments on thousands of EUR), 29 EUR is easy to justify. To replace one founder salary at about 4 000 EUR a month, roughly 140 paying companies are needed. The text shows no evidence that owners pay for software today, which caps this at 4 with medium confidence.
questions: What do the owners you know pay today for any app or accountant tool?
Would they pay yearly up front for a discount?
improve: Test 29 EUR against 49 EUR with the first ten owners; the pain may support more.

evidence: First channel: I will call them, then the regional trade group on Facebook
still know about 40 owners in my region
assumptions: Assuming the Facebook group has a few thousand members and allows posts from members.
rubrics.reasoning: A named first channel the founder already has access to, matched to a cheap product: forty phone calls cost nothing. The second channel, a regional trade group, is plausible for the next hundred. What is missing is anything repeatable beyond the region: no search, referral or partner channel is named. Score 4.
questions: Where do owners outside your region gather: national groups, suppliers, trade fairs?
improve: Build a referral into the product: the owner's customer sees the photo invoice and asks who made it.

evidence: Stage: idea and a clickable prototype, evenings only
photographs the site before and after, taps start and stop per job
assumptions: Assuming a standard mobile stack with photo upload, a timer and PDF invoice generation; no AI needed for the core.
rubrics.reasoning: The first slice is obvious: a timer per job, photo upload, and a PDF invoice sent by email. All of it is proven technology and cheap to build with coding agents. Risks are operational, not technical: Polish invoicing rules (numbering, VAT, the coming e-invoicing system) and offline use on site. Evenings-only pace is the main constraint, so the first version should skip accounting integration. Score 4.
questions: Have you checked what a compliant Polish invoice needs, including the national e-invoicing rules?
Does the app need to work without signal on site?
improve: Ship invoice as PDF by email first; integrate with accounting software only after ten paying owners.

evidence: I ran a crew like this for six years
assumptions: Assuming an AI-free product, so the vendor-feature risk is low; a generic field-service tool could still add a Polish invoice template.
rubrics.reasoning: Nothing stops a copy on day one. What can build over time: the history of photo-backed jobs per customer (a switching cost once a year of records is inside), and trust in a small niche that larger field-service vendors do not serve in Polish. Founder insight helps but is not a moat. Score 3: none yet, plausible later.
questions: What will the app know after a year that a new entrant would not?
improve: Make the job history useful to the owner's customer too (a shared record), which raises the cost of leaving.

evidence: I ran a crew like this for six years
Clickable prototype, about 8 hours a week, can go a year without revenue.
assumptions: Assuming the founder can build or has a developer; the text does not say who makes the app.
rubrics.reasoning: Six years of running the exact customer's business is the kind of insight the market cannot read in a blog post, and the owner network is an unfair advantage for the first sales. Time is thin, eight hours a week, but runway is a year without revenue, which covers validation. The gap is build capacity: the text never says who writes the code. Score 4.
questions: Who builds the app, and how many hours a week can they give it?
improve: Decide now whether to pay for a first build or partner with a developer for equity; eight hours a week is enough to sell, not to build and sell.

evidence: the owner gets a ready invoice the same evening
assumptions: Assuming Polish jurisdiction and the national e-invoicing obligation applying to small companies in the coming years.
Assuming site photos may include people or private property.
rubrics.reasoning: Two risks matter. Invoicing is regulated in Poland, and the national e-invoicing system will change what a valid invoice is; the product must follow it or hand off to accounting software. Photos of private gardens and occasionally people raise GDPR questions, manageable with retention limits and consent in the terms. No platform dependency beyond the app stores. Nothing here stops the idea. Score 4.
questions: Have you confirmed the e-invoicing timeline for companies of this size?
improve: Delete or blur photos after a set period and say so in the terms.

changes.why: Score stands. Confidence stays high: the segment, the buyer and the first forty contacts are all in the text.

critic.notes: The scores track the text. The one soft spot is monetization: no evidence yet that these owners pay for any software, so medium confidence there is right.

synthesis.summary: FieldNote turns a landscaping crew's photos and hours into a same-evening invoice for small Polish owners. The customer, the pain and the first channel are concrete, and the founder has lived the business. The open points are whether owners pay for software at all, how big the national market is, and who builds the app at eight hours a week.
synthesis.riskiestAssumption: Owners of 2 to 8 person crews will pay 29 EUR a month for faster, photo-backed invoicing instead of keeping the notebook and WhatsApp.

experiments.name: Ten calls, three pre-sales
experiments.what: Call ten of the forty owners. Describe the same-evening photo invoice and ask for 29 EUR up front for the first month, refundable.

experiments.name: Concierge invoice
experiments.what: For two owners, do it by hand for two weeks: they send photos and hours on WhatsApp, you send a finished invoice the same evening.
experiments.metric: Both owners ask to continue after two weeks and days-to-payment drops versus their last month.

experiments.name: Software spend check
experiments.what: In the same calls, ask what each owner pays today for any app, tool or accountant service.
experiments.metric: At least 6 of 10 already pay for something monthly.

openQuestions: Who builds the app, and how many hours a week can they give it?
What do the owners you know pay today for any app or accountant tool?
How many landscaping companies of this size exist in Poland?
Have you confirmed the e-invoicing timeline for companies of this size?
Which three apps have the owners you know tried and dropped, and why?
